titleStmt.title: Design and implementation of two medical escape rooms: an educational case study

analytic.title: Design and implementation of two medical escape rooms: an educational case study

div.p: Background: Escape rooms (ERs) have become increasingly popular as an interactive educational experience, especially in medical education. We present an educational case study covering the design, implementation, and evaluation of two medical ERs.

div.head: Approach:
div.p: We created ERs for senior medical students from Glasgow University on rotation at Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary. Students assessed and managed a patient presenting with either stroke or sepsis. The information gained during students' assessment 'unlocked' padlocks or generated codes providing further information or equipment. The ERs were evaluated following analysis of video recordings, debriefings, and student and faculty feedback.

Evaluation: Evaluation was focused on students' perceptions of the teaching experience, with changes made to the scenario design following student feedback and faculty reflection. Feedback was positive; students enjoyed the 'fun' nature of the learning experience. They felt they gained knowledge covering the subject areas and that the ERs also highlighted the importance of non-technical skills. We discuss the aspects of ER design and implementation that we learnt during the evaluation process.

div.head: Implications:
div.p: We have shown that medical ERs provide an immersive and engaging learning experience for students. We recognise a need for a more objective review of knowledge gained. We hope that by sharing our design and assessment of two medical ERs, we may inform and inspire other educators to consider ERs as an innovative learning experience.

div.head: Background
div.p: Escape rooms (ERs) were originally developed as a leisure activity. Participants are 'locked' in a room and given a series of puzzles or clues to solve to escape. The concept has been applied to several professional settings, including medical education (1)(2)(3)(4).

Scenario-based ERs are founded on experiential learning theory with reflective observation after the learning event (1,5). ERs make use of a concept called 'gamification' to motivate participants towards achieving planned objectives. Gamification is the use of game elements in a non-game setting. When done well, this can enhance adult learning, but if improperly applied it may be detrimental (2).

We present an educational case study from Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary (DGRI). DGRI is a 350-bed district general hospital which receives students from the University of Glasgow on general medical rotations. The local teaching programme includes a series of tutorials which are determined by the University of Glasgow curriculum. Small group teaching on the topics of 'weakness' and 'fever' takes place in the 4 th year. The local teaching faculty wanted to add experiential learning to build on existing knowledge and looked to the ER concept as an innovative method to provide this. Because Glasgow University has a spiral curriculum, with areas being revisited in subsequent years, ERs were also delivered to 5 th year students (6).

div.head: Approach
div.p: We created two ER scenarios based on the clinical presentations of sepsis (secondary to pneumonia) and ischaemic stroke, in line with the curriculum topics of 'fever' and 'weakness.' Local ER design was guided by ER literature and Joplin's five stage model of experiential learning (4,7-9), which recommends that for learners to gain the most from learning encounters, they should be designed to establish a focus, provide an active learning experience, and provide support, feedback, then a debrief. A structured brief sets the focus for the sessions. The second stage is student-led patient assessment. Support is provided during the game by clues, student peers and the teacher, who acts as the 'medical registrar.' The teacher also provides support before and after the game by ensuring mutual trust and psychological safety within the group. The absence of a helper in the room simulates the feeling of being alone with a patient during initial assessment, which the students will experience as an FY1. As in Joplin's model, feedback and debriefing are the final stages of our ER student experience (8).

Each scenario consists of a linear narrative, in which solving a clinical puzzle gives a code to unlock equipment or information required for the next step of the patient journey, during an allotted time of 60 minutes. The narrative is based on the diagnostic pathway of history, examination, investigation, diagnosis, and treatment. This breaks down the narrative into steps, with checkpoints to ensure attainment of learning objectives while progressing through the scenario (Figures 1 and2). We use our hospital's simulation suite as our ER, allowing us to observe students remotely and talk to them by intercom. A Clinical Teaching Fellow acts both as facilitator and medical registrar and can, if necessary, intervene to allow game play to progress if students are unable to solve a task. The facilitator controls the difficulty of the scenario, for example by interrupting participants to give further clinical tasks to prioritise (e.g., Figure 1 Task 10).

When running the scenarios, two students enter the ER with the patient surrogate, while two students act as remote helpers from an observation room with access to both the internet and hospital intranet. A Foundation Doctor acts as the patient surrogate. Manikins are used for clinical skills such as venepuncture. Cameras allow peers to watch the scenario remotely and facilitate recording for debriefing and evaluation purposes. We initially trialled both scenarios with Foundation Doctors, which gave us the opportunity to make changes using their feedback.

The creation of ER paperwork included a storyboard, set up guide, briefing and debriefing guide for facilitators, scripts for game characters, National Early Warning Score (NEWS) and fluid charts as required by the scenario, video consent forms and feedback forms. The latter consists of structured questions with free-text responses, covering aspects such as student perceived learning and design and delivery improvement suggestions. We evaluate and refine our ERs following analysis of video recordings of student briefs and debriefs, and review of feedback forms. Written consent is gained from participants for video recording.

div.head: Evaluation
div.p: We evaluated each scenario using a combination of student feedback and our own observations of student behaviour as they responded to the challenges set. Observations were based on 15 evaluations of 60 student encounters. The goal of evaluation was to review student experience, including subjective achievement of learning goals; critique the design and delivery of the ER; and Students' reactions to the experience were positive overall and the 'fun' nature of the learning experience was a theme across multiple debriefs. Several students reported reduced stress compared to traditional simulation experiences. Students said they felt they gained clinical knowledge and skills relevant to each case, with checkpoints providing additional objective feedback. Students also cited learning of non-technical skills. Student feedback and faculty reflection allowed us to understand the limitations of each scenario and prompted changes in the game format. Here we list some of our reflections and learnings:

div.head: Keep clues simple
div.p: A student comment, 'I didn't understand the question' prompted re-evaluation of our clues and how we explained them in the ER briefing. The facilitator noted one clue had required several attempts, so it was discussed with students in the debrief and modified prior to the next ER (Figure 3). In medicine the correct answer is not always 'black or white', but codes are either right or wrong. We realised this meant that a clinically insignificant misinterpretation or rounding error by the students could be the difference between success and failure. Showing clue examples in the prebrief helped students understand the format of the clues (Figure 4).

div.head: Figure 3
div.p: Keeping clues simple. Clue A asks students to demonstrate their knowledge of, or their ability to discover, the upper limit of normal for the QTc interval in a male patient, and the KDIGO criteria for acute kidney injury (AKI) stage 1. It quickly became apparent when we play-tested this scenario that these questions were not sufficiently specific. Different sources quote different normal ranges for QTc and AKI stage 1 can be defined either by a serum creatinine that is greater than 26umol/l or 1.5-1.9x above baseline, with both answers being correct. The learning outcomes are the same in Clue B, but these problems have been overcome by simplifying the questions.

div.head: Set clear expectations
div.p: The student comment, 'I wasn't sure if the job was to keep the patient alive and treat them or actually escape', informed consideration of how the student's role within the ER was introduced. The faculty reflected on the reasons for this student's experience, combining it with a re-review of the brief. It was identified that further structured briefing was needed. The ER briefing has two purposes. Firstly, it should create a psychologically safe learning environment in line with adult learning principles (7). Secondly, it should explain the rules and parameters of gameplay. In light of this student's comment we developed a briefing guide for each scenario (Figure 5).

div.head: Figure 5.
div.p: Suggested briefing structure for medical ERs

div.head: Importance of professionalism
div.p: Professionalism played a key part in setting expectations for each scenario (Figure 5, point 3). This was felt important to ensure that the game element did not override acceptable behaviour within a clinical environment. The ER has a time limit and a leader board, and the teaching faculty noticed that students did not always use aseptic technique when rushing to complete procedural tasks. During the brief, the faculty ensured participants were aware that safe clinical care was required to escape the room. If inappropriate behaviour was seen, it was addressed at the time by the 'medical registrar' and students were asked to repeat tasks or given support to do so. If this was not possible it was discussed in the debrief.
4. Consider how participants can ask for help.

In our early ERs we introduced the concept of the 'unhelpful' medical registrar to encourage problemsolving within the peer group before asking for help from a senior colleague. In clinical practice junior doctors are encouraged to seek senior help when faced with an unwell patient, but we found that participants seldom called the medical registrar even when they ran out of ideas. When we changed this to a 'helpful but busy' medical registrar who would prompt participants to review local guidelines before giving further advice, students did contact the registrar when they were concerned, demonstrating desirable professional behaviours.

div.head: Resource costs
div.p: We also considered resource costs. Setup time for an escape room was 90 to 120 minutes, compared to 30 minutes for simulation. Once the ERs were designed and initial equipment purchased there was minimal resource cost per scenario, as most items were re-used except for clinical procedural equipment. The minimum faculty numbers for an ER were one teaching faculty member and one patient actor, with clues removing the need for a confederate.

div.head: Implications
div.p: ERs are now established as an immersive teaching and learning experience at our hospital. Locally, educators have learnt key lessons during the evaluation period. The small number of faculty members required is attractive. The next steps are to consider more detailed evaluation of the student experience and objective review of students' attainment of learning outcomes. Expanding the local ER programme for students from other universities, including Edinburgh and Dundee, is a longer-term aim.

ER literature generally describes single scenarios (4,(11)(12)(13). A novel aspect of our case study was the presentation of two different scenarios (Figures 1 and2), developed to cover different presentations and learning objectives. A further novel aspect is the presentation of a structured ER debriefing guide (Figure 5) which may help other educators transfer their experience of briefing and debriefing in simulation to the ER context.

figure.figDesc: following each cycle allowed us to modify the scenarios if required to maximise the learning experience. In this way, we met level 1 and 2 criteria of the Kirkpatrick Model of Evaluation, in which level 1 captures participants' reactions to the training experience, and level 2 determines what the participants learned(10).
